title: Endophthalmitis: The Ultimate Clinical Compendium
summary: A sight-threatening emergency involving severe intraocular inflammation, most commonly due to bacterial or fungal infection. Rapid diagnosis, prompt intravitreal intervention, and adherence to evidence-based protocols are critical for visual salvage.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Endophthalmitis is defined as severe inflammation of the inner coats of the eye, specifically the vitreous and aqueous humors. It is categorized as Exogenous (inoculation from the environment, e.g., surgery, trauma) or Endogenous (hematogenous spread from a distant focus). It represents the most feared complication in ophthalmic surgery.

rows: S. epidermidis (70%), S. aureus, Strep spp.
High risk with intraocular foreign body

sections.title: Pathophysiology Process
content: 1. Microbial Inoculation: Pathogens enter the vitreous cavity (exogenous) or uveal tract (endogenous).
2. Proliferation: Microbes multiply rapidly in the nutrient-rich vitreous, escaping early immune detection.
3. Toxogenesis: Release of bacterial exotoxins and enzymes (proteases) that directly damage photoreceptors.
4. Host Response: Massive influx of neutrophils (PMNs) and release of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha).
5. Retinal Destruction: Bystander damage from host inflammatory mediators leads to irreversible retinal necrosis.
6. Organization: Chronic inflammation leads to cyclitic membrane formation and tractional retinal detachment.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Lid Edema and Chemosis: Significant soft tissue swelling.
Conjunctival Injection: Intense circumcorneal flush.
Corneal Edema: Due to toxic endothelial damage.
Hypopyon: Layered WBCs in the anterior chamber (present in 75-85%).
Fibrinous Membrane: Dense AC reaction often obscuring the pupil.
Vitritis: Dense vitreous cells and debris causing loss of red reflex.
Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD): Suggests advanced retinal or optic nerve damage.

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAGS
content: Pain that is out of proportion to clinical signs.
Sudden, profound loss of vision (Light Perception or worse).
Rapidly progressing hypopyon within hours.
Loss of Red Reflex or inability to visualize fundus.
Proptosis or limited motility (suggests panophthalmitis).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Clinical Suspicion: History of recent surgery or trauma + pain/vision loss.
2. B-Scan Ultrasonography: Essential if fundus is obscured. Look for vitreal opacities, membranes, or RD.
3. Vitreous Tap/Biopsy: Gold standard. Needle aspiration (0.1ml) or undiluted vitreous cutter sample.
4. Aqueous Tap: Lower yield than vitreous but easier to perform (0.1ml).
5. Microbiological Processing: Immediate Gram/Giemsa stain, culture on Blood, Chocolate, Sabouraud, and Thioglycolate.
6. Molecular Diagnosis: PCR for 16S rDNA (high sensitivity, especially if pre-treated).

sections.title: EVS Treatment Algorithm (Based on Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study)

branches: Vision Hand Motions (HM) or Better: Tap and Inject Antibiotics
Vision Light Perception (LP): Immediate Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) + Antibiotics
Systemic Antibiotics: Found not useful (Amikacin/Ceftazidime) in EVS

sections.title: Surgical Technique: PPV Steps
content: 1. Anesthesia: Retrobulbar or general (if severe pain/uncooperative).
2. Trocar Placement: Careful 23G/25G/27G entry; caution with hypotony.
3. Sample Collection: Obtain undiluted vitreous sample before turning on infusion.
4. Core Vitrectomy: Clear central opacities to improve antibiotic distribution.
5. Avoid PVD Induction: The retina is extremely necrotic/friable; do not induce PVD.
6. Antibiotic Injection: Controlled injection into the mid-vitreous cavity.

sections.title: Post-Traumatic Specifics
content: Bacillus cereus: Most common in soil-related trauma; causes rapid panophthalmitis in 24h.
IOFB: Retained foreign bodies increase risk by 10x.
Clostridium: Rare but causes 'Gas Gangrene' of the eye with rapid vision loss.
Immediate PPV: Often indicated earlier in trauma than in post-cataract cases.

content.explanation: Vision (LP vs HM), Vitreous (Tap vs Vitrectomy), Vancomycin (The cornerstone of therapy).

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: Povidone-Iodine 5%: Only proven prophylactic measure to reduce endophthalmitis risk.
Intracameral Cefuroxime (1mg/0.1ml): ESCRS study showed 5x reduction in post-op infection.
C. acnes: Suspect if there is a 'white plaque' on the posterior capsule months after surgery.
Klebsiella Endogenous: Often presents with a 'hypopyon of the posterior pole' (subretinal abscess).

sections.title: Complications & Sequelae
content: Retinal Detachment (Tractional or Rhegmatogenous).
Phthisis Bulbi: Hypotony and shrinkage of the globe.
Secondary Glaucoma: Due to inflammatory debris or PAS.
Cyclitic Membrane: Resulting in ciliary body detachment.
Evisceration/Enucleation: Required if panophthalmitis occurs or for intractable pain.
